UPDATE: Impeachment

This week the House voted to impeach President Trump. Impeachment in the House and a trial in the Senate are all laid out in the Constitution (Article 1, Sections 2 and 3). However, the process and precedent for impeachment are relatively vague, particularly when it comes to impeachment and removal proceedings for presidents.

This marks only the fourth time in our nation’s history a president has been brought up on impeachment charges in the House. Presidents Andrew Johnson, Richard Nixon, and Bill Clinton were all subject to House investigations into impeachment. But only Presidents Johnson and Clinton were formally impeached by the House, and neither was removed from office by the Senate. All impeachments are sad moments for our nation, but our Founders laid out a process to investigate wrongdoing for members of the Executive and Judicial Branches.

Impeachment is extremely rare in our nation’s history, but this is the first time the House of Representatives has not filed articles of impeachment over a specific federal crime, instead the House charged the President with abuse of power and obstruction of Congress. The first accusation is that President Trump intended to inappropriately influence government leaders in Ukraine to investigate Hunter Biden, the son of the former Vice President; though the government of Ukraine did not actually carry out any investigation or believe that President Trump was pressuring it to do so. The second accusation is that the President did not turn over every document the House requested and/or encourage every White House staff member to testify in the impeachment investigation during the last month of the proceedings; though the White House did turn over the transcript of the phone call at the center of the debate within 24 hours of when it was requested.

This is actually the second time the House of Representatives has attempted to impeach the President this year. In July the House voted to open up impeachment proceedings, well before there was any conversation about Ukraine, but that vote failed. Many members of the House also wanted to impeach the President for election conspiracy with Russia, until the Special Counsel investigation found that the President and his team did not conspire with Russia in the 2016 election.

In January the Senate will move into the trial phase of impeachment proceedings. That will be the first time the President and the House will be given equal time to present their side of the story. When the trial begins, both sides will give their opinions and present their facts, and then the senators will be allowed to ask questions of the President and the House “managers.” The trial will probably take at least two weeks. I have heard some people call the senators “jurors” for the impeachment trial, but actually that is not true. While each senator will take an oath and be required to make a decision on the case, we can research facts on our own and talk openly about the case. I do not have to ignore the details I already know, but I should and will listen to both sides. At this point, I have not seen any evidence of a crime or any action deserving of removing a president from office, especially just a few months before a national election.
